name: Battle of Carrhae
info: A Parthian cavalry army under Surena defeated the Roman army of Marcus Licinius Crassus near Carrhae in 53 BCE; Crassus was killed, most of his men were killed or captured, and Parthia later invaded Syria and Armenia.

facts.date: 9 June 53 BCE, the date given by Ovid in Book 6 of the Fasti
facts.place: Near the ancient town of Carrhae, present-day Harran, Turkey, on the plain of northern Mesopotamia
facts.sides: The Roman Republic under Marcus Licinius Crassus, with seven legions of about 28,000 to 35,000 heavy infantry, about 4,000 light infantry and 4,000 cavalry according to Plutarch; the Parthian Empire under the spahbod Surena, with roughly 10,000 men
facts.outcome: Crassus was killed when truce negotiations turned violent. Most of his army was killed or captured; Plutarch gives about 20,000 killed and 10,000 captured, and Parthian casualties as minimal.

t: Surena's horse archers stayed out of reach of the Roman javelins, and the Romans' close formations could not drive them off or fight back, while his cataphracts charged whenever the Romans loosened their ranks.

Crassus refused Artavasdes II's offer of a route through Armenia and of reinforcements, and marched straight through Mesopotamia; Surena, whose force was heavily outnumbered, had been sent only to scout and harass him.
Plutarch gives about 20,000 Roman dead and 10,000 prisoners. Gaius Cassius Longinus led about 10,000 survivors back to Syria and defended the province against Parthian attacks.
dyk: The Parthians kept up their supply of arrows by using thousands of camels, which Crassus had hoped would run out before his legionaries gave way.
ev: Crassus, Pompey and Caesar renew their alliance at Ravenna and Luca, and Crassus arranges to have Syria as his province
Crassus invades the Parthian client-state of Osroene while Surena defeats and executes Mithridates IV at Seleucia
In the spring Crassus rejects Armenia's offer and marches through Mesopotamia
Surena's horse archers and cataphracts defeat the Romans near Carrhae, and Publius Crassus dies with his force
Crassus is killed at a truce meeting, and Cassius leads about 10,000 survivors back to Syria
A Parthian invasion is stopped and repulsed by Publius Ventidius Bassus
Mark Antony invades Parthia in the Atropatene campaign, which also fails

sections.background:
The war grew out of the arrangements of the First Triumvirate of Marcus Licinius Crassus, Pompeius Magnus and Julius Caesar. At meetings at Ravenna and Luca in March and April 56 BCE the three agreed to secure legislation prolonging Caesar's Gallic command and to put Crassus and Pompey forward for a second joint consulship. The faction won the consulship, and the Lex Trebonia gave the two outgoing consuls proconsulships of five years. Pompey received the Spanish provinces, and Crassus arranged to have Syria with the transparent intention of going to war with Parthia.

In Parthia a war of succession had broken out in 57 BCE, after King Phraates III was killed by his sons Orodes II and Mithridates IV. Orodes forced Mithridates to flee to Aulus Gabinius, the Roman proconsul of Syria, who abandoned plans to use him and intervened in Egypt instead. Gabinius's successor Crassus also sought to ally with Mithridates and invaded the Parthian client-state of Osroene in 54 BCE, but spent most of his time waiting for reinforcements while Surena besieged, defeated and executed Mithridates at Seleucia on the Tigris.

Crassus was about 62 and very wealthy. Ancient sources, particularly Plutarch, name greed as his motive. Erich S. Gruen believes he meant to enrich the public treasury, while most modern historians point to greed, envy of Pompey's exploits and rivalry. Cicero called the war nulla causa, as Parthia had a treaty with Rome, and the tribune Ateius Capito performed a public ritual of execration as Crassus prepared to leave. Crassus left Rome on 14 November 55 BCE.
sections.forces:
Crassus raised his army in Syria with his own wealth. According to Plutarch he assembled seven legions, about 28,000 to 35,000 heavy infantry, with about 4,000 light infantry and 4,000 cavalry, including 1,000 Gallic horse brought by his son Publius. Artavasdes II of Armenia advised him to go through Armenia to avoid the desert and offered a further 10,000 cavalry and 30,000 infantry. Crassus refused twice, the second time when Artavasdes came to his camp with 6,000 cavalry, and chose the direct route through Mesopotamia.

Orodes divided the Parthian army. He took most of it, mainly foot archers with a small amount of cavalry, to punish the Armenians, and sent an all-cavalry force under the spahbod Surena to scout and harass Crassus. Plutarch describes it as a thousand mail-clad horsemen and a still greater number of light-armed cavalry. With slaves and vassals Surena's expedition numbered ten thousand, supported by a baggage train of 1,000 camels. Orodes did not expect it to defeat Crassus and wanted only to delay him.

Crassus took directions from the Osroene chieftain Ariamnes, who was in Parthian pay and urged him to attack at once, saying the Parthians were weak. Plutarch says Ariamnes led the army into the most desolate part of the desert, far from water. Gregory Hospodor has found that Crassus followed a well-travelled caravan route past several towns on the Balikh River, with ample water from spring runoff, which casts doubt on the claim of sabotage. On 9 June the scouts were found slain and a large force of cavalry was approaching.
sections.course:
On hearing of the Parthians the Roman army panicked. Cassius recommended the traditional order, infantry in the centre and cavalry on the wings. Crassus first agreed but then formed a hollow square, each side of twelve cohorts, which guarded against outflanking at the cost of mobility. At a stream his generals advised camping, but Publius persuaded Crassus to confront the Parthians at once.

The Parthians beat hollow drums, and Surena's cataphracts dropped cloths from their armour to reveal it. Surena judged a charge would not yet break the Romans and sent his horse archers round the square, beyond the range of the pila. His skirmishers were driven back. When the Romans advanced, the horse archers retreated and shot as they withdrew. The legionaries formed the testudo, which restricted their melee fighting, and the cataphracts charged repeatedly, causing panic and heavy casualties. When the Romans loosened their ranks, the cataphracts withdrew and the horse archers shot at the exposed men.

Crassus hoped the arrows would run out, but Surena resupplied them with camels. Crassus sent Publius with 1,300 Gallic cavalry, 500 archers and eight cohorts against the horse archers. They feigned retreat and drew him off, the cataphracts then confronted his force and the horse archers cut off its retreat. Publius and his officers threw themselves on their swords, and only 500 Gauls were taken alive. Crassus was shown his son's head on a spear. The attacks went on until nightfall, and a ragged retreat to Carrhae left 4,000 wounded, who were killed next morning. Four cohorts lost in the dark were surrounded on a hill, and only 20 Romans survived.
sections.aftermath:
The next day Surena offered to negotiate and proposed a truce allowing the Romans to return to Syria in exchange for all territory east of the Euphrates. Crassus was reluctant to meet, but his troops threatened to mutiny. At the meeting a Parthian pulled at Crassus's reins and violence broke out in which Crassus and his generals were killed. Parthians allegedly poured molten gold down his throat, mocking his greed, and Plutarch reports that his severed head was used in a performance of Euripides' Bacchae at a banquet before the king. The remaining Romans tried to flee, but most were captured or killed. Plutarch gives about 20,000 killed and 10,000 captured, and says Parthian casualties were minimal.

The Parthians captured several legionary eagles. Plutarch also mentions that they dressed the prisoner who most resembled Crassus as a woman and paraded him through Parthia, ordering the other prisoners to hail him as Imperator, in mockery of a Roman triumph. The 10,000 prisoners appear to have been deported to Alexandria Margiana (Merv) near the north-eastern border, where they reportedly married local people.

Orodes II defeated the Armenians and took their country, but Surena's victory made the king jealous, and he had Surena executed. His son Pacorus then led an unsuccessful campaign into Syria. Gaius Cassius Longinus, a quaestor under Crassus, led about 10,000 survivors back to Syria and governed it for two more years as proquaestor. He resisted the Parthian siege of Antioch and ambushed Pacorus's army at Antigonea as it retreated, killing the Parthian second-in-command Osaces, and Cicero praised him.
sections.sources:
The account of the fighting rests largely on Plutarch, whose figures for the armies and for the casualties are the ones usually repeated, and who blames Crassus for every aspect of the defeat, particularly his tactics. Ovid gives the date of 9 June in Book 6 of the Fasti. Plutarch is also the source of the tales of the molten gold, the performance of the Bacchae and the false Crassus paraded through Parthia.

Historians dispute several points. Hospodor questions Plutarch's suggestion that Ariamnes led Crassus into a waterless desert on purpose, and finds Plutarch's account of Crassus's second meeting with Artavasdes questionable. Some historians describe arrows partly penetrating the Roman shields and nailing them to the limbs of the legionaries and their feet to the ground, while Plutarch wrote that arrows passed through every kind of cover, and others state that most wounds were non-fatal hits to exposed limbs. It is also uncertain whether Surena himself or an emissary went to ask for the peace conference. In the 1940s Homer H. Dubs proposed that the people of Liqian in China descended from the Roman prisoners; no coins, weapons or other artefacts of a Roman presence have been found at Zhelaizhai, and the vast majority of historians do not accept it.
sections.legacy:
The Parthian capture of the golden eagles was considered a grave moral defeat and an evil omen for the Romans. When Caesar was assassinated in 44 BCE he was planning a retaliatory war. The battle was one of the first major battles between Rome and Parthia, and it led Parthia to invade Syria and Armenia several times, with varying success. Rome also realised that its legionaries could not fight Parthian cavalry effectively without support in open terrain.

An old theory holds that the death of Crassus, with that of Julia, Pompey's wife and Caesar's daughter, in 54 BCE, severed the ties between Caesar and Pompey and ended the First Triumvirate, so that Caesar's civil war followed. Several historians note the time that passed between Crassus's death and the outbreak of civil war. Stern has claimed that the death nearly cut the links the Triumvirate had with the aristocracy, leaving the state vulnerable to friction that turned into civil war. In a regional context the battle had little negative impact for Rome in the long term: the Parthian invasion of 40 BCE was stopped and repulsed by Publius Ventidius Bassus, and Antony's invasion of Parthia in 36 BCE, though it also ended in failure, was not prevented.

Hospodor argues that Crassus is to blame tactically only for the poorly organised retreat, and that blaming him alone oversimplifies the result, which exposed both the strengths and the weaknesses of the Roman military system of the late Republic. He suggests Crassus's adherence to doctrine may have led him to trust heavy infantry against cavalry.

summary: At Carrhae in 53 BCE a Parthian cavalry force under Surena, using horse archers and cataphracts, defeated the Roman army of Marcus Licinius Crassus. Crassus was killed at a truce meeting, and Plutarch gives about 20,000 Roman dead and 10,000 prisoners.
references: Gareth Sampson, The Defeat of Rome in the East: Crassus, the Parthians, and the Disastrous battle of Carrhae, 53 BC (Casemate, 2008)
Neilson Debevoise, A Political History of Parthia (University of Chicago Press, 1938)
notes: The article contradicts itself on Artavasdes II: it says he defected to the Parthian side when Orodes invaded Armenia, yet he later visits Crassus, and sends a message that the main Parthian army is in Armenia. I left the defection out.

Plutarch's figures: 28,000 to 35,000 heavy infantry, with 4,000 light infantry and 4,000 cavalry. The lead says seven legions; the article's Armenian 'about 6,000 cavalry' appears both as support on the march and at the second visit.
The Parthian strength is given as 'roughly 10,000' in the battle section and 'ten thousand in total including slaves and vassals' earlier; the 1,000 mail-clad horsemen is Plutarch's.

Left out as garbled: 'Marcus Licinius Crassus the surviving son of Crassus would have been among the Roman forces' (the second son is not named elsewhere); 'Gaius Stern' (probably Gaius Stern is a garbled name; I wrote only 'Stern'); 'the following retaliatory Pompeian-Parthian invasion of 40 BC in 40 BC'; 'Antony's Atropatene campaign'.
The article has Parthia's strongest figure on cataphracts, 'a thousand mail-clad horsemen', as Plutarch's; it does not say how many horse archers.

Left out: Rob Gifford and Alfred Duggan's novel on the prisoners, the Fish-scale formation of Dubs, Hospodor's speculation on Armenian two-front war, details of Ichnae and Zenodotium, the 7,000 garrison, Crassus 'nearly catatonic', and the praise words in the lead ('crushing', 'decisively').

Cut for length: Stern's point on Crassus's tie to Metellus Pius Scipio, and Hospodor's remark that no one at the council of war proposed moving to terrain less favourable to cavalry. The Antigonea ambush has no year in the article, so no event carries it.
